title: Patient complaints in dentistry: A qualitative meta-synthesis
content:
by Lorraine Snyman, Thomas Corne Postma, Werdie Van Staden

Introduction

Patient complaints in dentistry concern their dissatisfaction, safety concerns, quality of care, and challenges within the patient-practitioner relationship. Whilst existing research of these complaints has largely focused on quantitative analysis of regulatory complaints and malpractice, these studies capture little of the meaning that patients express in their complaints. This study synthesized a qualitative understanding of patient complaints across various dentistry settings.

Method

This qualitative meta-synthesis followed the six-step approach of Sandelowski and Barroso, drawing on previously published qualitative findings from various studies that constituted a higher-order case as suggested by Hoon’s design framework. Data was sourced through a comprehensive search of health databases (MEDLINE, PsycINFO, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL). From studies found suitable upon appraisal, findings were subjected to reflexive thematic analysis. The resulting synthesis is reported according to the PRISMA guidelines extended for qualitative evidence synthesis.

Results

From an initial 857 studies, 19 met criteria for inclusion. Complaints reflected patient experiences in four inter-related domains of concern, namely, 1) impeded access to dental care, 2) unsatisfactory communication, interactions and attitudes, 3) deficient clinical treatment, and 4) unethical and unprofessional conduct. These domains may be understood as underlying processes in which patients experienced threats to trust, patient agency and autonomy, relational security, and that professional and ethical obligations have been breached. They may also be understood as signals of broader systemic and relational functioning.

Conclusion

Our findings suggest that complaints may reflect breakdowns in the fiduciary patient-practitioner relationship and constitute an important source of insight into the relational and systemic conditions necessary for trustworthy, person-centered dental care.

Clinical relevance

The four domains yielded in this synthesis may inform dentists and health systems on the scope of compromised relationships and systemic deficiencies as well as efforts to improve the quality of dental care and reduce patient complaints.
